annotations.question: Assuming SBAC has to refinance its debt maturities in 2025 and 2026 at a 10% interest rate, and assuming this debt had a 4% interest rate before, what is the incremental interest expense that the firm will face going forwards?
solution:
## Locate the relevant table.
Open the SBAC 10-K for Fiscal 2024 and go to page 80 of the document. Go to section 11 of the notes to the financial statements titled "11. Debt". This section will contain three tables. Go to the second table (which is at the bottom of page 80 of the pdf) which is labeled "for the year ended December 31" and lists the years of maturity and the dollar values of debt maturing in those years ("in thousands" - located on top right of the table). This is essentially the debt maturity schedule for the company.

## Locate the relevant securities and extract principal balance.
In this second table (the debt maturity schedule for the company), extract the values for debt maturing in the years 2025 and 2026. This will be found in the table labeled "2025" and "2026" respectively. Debt maturing in 2025 = 1,188,000 ("in thousands").
Debt maturing in 2026 = 1,938,000.

## Sum the total amount maturing over 2025 and 2026.
Sum the values for debt maturing in 2025 and 2026. Total debt maturing in the next two years = Debt maturing in 2025 + Debt maturing in 2026 = 1,188,000 + 1,938,000 = 3,126,000 (in thousands).

## Calculate the current interest expense given a 4% interest rate.
Multiply the total debt maturing in 2025 and 2026 by 4% to get the implied current interest expense.
Current interest expense given 4% interest rate = 3,126,000 * 4% = 125,040 (in thousands)

## Calculate the refinanced interest expense given a 10% interest rate.
Multiply the total debt maturing in 2025 and 2026 by 10% to get the implied refinanced interest expense.
refinanced interest expense given 10% interest rate = 3,126,000 * 10% = 312,600 (in thousands)

## Calculate the difference in interest expense.
Subtract the current interest expense given 4% interest from the refinanced interest expense given 10% interest to get the difference in interest expense. 
difference in interest expense = 312,600 - 125,040 = 
187,560 (in thousands)

annotations.question: What was SoFi's adjusted EBITDA in 2024?
solution:
## Identify net income for 2024.
SoFi Technologies, Inc. To begin, you locate SoFi’s net income for fiscal year 2024, Net Income (Loss), and Adjusted EBITDA on page 95 of the 10-K, where a table labeled “($ in thousands)” presents financial performance across 2024, 2023, and 2022. The “Net income (loss)” figure for 2024 is $498,665 thousand.

## Add expenses to find EBITDA.
The next step is to add back standard non-cash and non-operating expenses to move from net income to EBITDA.  
Net Income (Loss) and Adjusted EBITDA  
On page 95, SoFi provides a reconciliation of GAAP net income to non-GAAP measures, including the values we need in thousands. These include "Interest expense – corporate borrowings" at $48,346 thousand. "Depreciation and Amortization" at $203,498 thousand. "Share-based expense" at $246,152 thousand. These are all adjustments you need to incorporate when calculating EBITDA, as they do not reflect ongoing core operating performance.

## Subtract the tax benefit.
Net Income (Loss) and Adjusted EBITDA are also on page 95. Find the line "Income tax (benefit) expense". Its value for 2024 is $(265,320) thousand. Because this tax item artificially inflates GAAP net income and EBITDA excludes tax effects, we subtract this benefit from our running total.

## Adjust for non-recurring expenses.
Net income (loss) and adjusted EBITDA. To get adjusted EBITDA, you then include further adjustments for one-time or non-core items, again disclosed on page 95 to reflect 2024. Within this table, the line titled "Restructuring charges" shows an amount of $1,530 thousand for 2024. The line labeled "Impairment expense" has no adjustment for 2024 as it is blank, so no figure is added. The line "Foreign currency impact of highly inflationary subsidiaries" reports an amount of $1,683 thousand for 2024. The line "Transaction-related expense" reflects an amount of $615 thousand for 2024. The line "Servicing rights — change in valuation inputs or assumptions" shows a negative adjustment of $(6,280) thousand for 2024. The line "Residual interests classified as debt — change in valuation inputs or assumptions" shows a positive adjustment of $108 thousand for 2024. The line "Gain on extinguishment of debt" shows a negative adjustment of $(62,517) thousand for 2024. Each of these amounts should be incorporated into the adjusted EBITDA calculation as appropriate, either adding positive adjustments or subtracting negative ones.

## Sum all the adjustments.
We now use the figures we found to sum the adjustments to EBITDA: $498,665 thousand + $48,346 thousand + $203,498 thousand + $246,152 thousand + $1,530 thousand + $1,683 thousand + $615 thousand − $265,320 thousand − $6,280 thousand + $108 thousand − $62,517 thousand =  
$666,480 thousand

annotations.question: Estimate the total number of physical assets deployed by Samsara’s Core Customers in 2023, assuming each customer uses 2 applications per asset and ARR per asset–application is $4,000.
solution:
## Retrieve ARR attributable to Core Customers.
Page 64 (Our Customers / Key Business Metrics) reports that as of January 28, 2023 Samsara had more than 19,000 Core Customers and $795,053 thousand of total annual recurring revenue (ARR), and that approximately 95% of ARR came from Core Customers. Core-Customer ARR is therefore about 0.95 × $795,053 thousand ≈ $755,300 thousand.

## Identify the pricing structure of subscriptions.
Samsara’s “Our Business Model” section on page 63 explains that each physical asset and each application is a separate subscription unit that contributes to ARR. As stated in the question, each asset uses 2 applications, so each physical asset corresponds to two asset–application subscriptions.

## Set up the equation for the number of assets.
Let x be the number of physical assets. With 2 applications per asset, the number of asset–application subscriptions is 2x. Each asset–application generates $4,000 of ARR, so total Core-Customer ARR equals 2x × $4,000 = $8,000x.

## Solve for the number of physical assets.
Set $8,000x equal to Core-Customer ARR: $8,000x = $755,300,350. Solving, x = $755,300,350 / $8,000 ≈ 94,412.5 physical assets.

annotations.question: If Robert Half International implemented a working capital optimization initiative in 2019 that reduced accounts receivable days by 5 days while keeping the same level of net service revenues as 2018, what would be the resulting one-time cash flow improvement in millions of dollars?
solution:

## Determine target accounts receivable days.
The target accounts receivable days would be 45.02 days (50.02 days - 5 days) based on the 5-day reduction mentioned in the question. This represents the new efficiency target for the accounts receivable collection process.

## Calculate the new accounts receivable balance.
With 45.02 days of accounts receivable, the new balance would be (Net Service Revenues ÷ 365) × New AR Days = ($5,800,271 thousand ÷ 365) × 45.02 days = $715,096 thousand. This represents the reduced investment in accounts receivable after the optimization initiative.

## Determine the cash flow improvement.
The cash flow improvement would be the difference between the current and new accounts receivable balances: $794,446 thousand - $715,096 thousand = $79,350 thousand or $79.35 million. This is the one-time cash release from reducing the accounts receivable days by 5 days.
$79.35 million

The OKLO 2024 10-K document requires users to access page 84 to view the Fair Value of Common Stock section which contains the stock option award activity summary for the year ending December 31, 2024. ## Apply the Treasury Stock Method assumption.
The problem requires us to use $6.00 as the average market price per share for 2024. The treasury stock method calculates the net dilutive effect of in-the-money options. The calculation of exercise proceeds requires us to determine the number of shares that can be bought back with exercise funds before subtracting them from the total number of outstanding options. The calculation of exercise proceeds requires the formula Options Outstanding multiplied by Weighted Average Exercise Price. The calculation of incremental dilution requires us to subtract repurchased shares from total options outstanding which equals Options Outstanding − Repurchased Shares = 9,470,382 − 3,077,874.15 = 6,392,507.85.

## Final conclusion.
The treasury stock method requires a $6.00 average share price to calculate the additional shares that should be included in Fully Diluted Shares Outstanding (FDSO) for December 31, 2024.  
6,392,507.85 shares.

annotations.question: Assume the company uses LIFO accounting and the LIFO reserve increased by $15,213 thousand during the year. What is the difference in gross margin under LIFO and FIFO accounting? Round your answer to the nearest hundredth, e.g., 32.48%.

To bring net income to a break-even point, assuming expenses remain constant at $9,617 million, revenue would have to increase by approximately  
46.578265424%

Execution and clearing expenses grow at 5% per year for two years. $386 times (1.05)^2 equals $386 times 1.1025 equals $425.57 million.

$1,471.0 minus $425.57 equals $1,045.43 million.

## Reinvest 10% of each year's gross profit at 3% compound.
2023 gross profit: $1,360 minus $386 equals $974 million. 10% is $97.4 million. Held 2 years at 3%: $97.4 times (1.03)^2 equals $97.4 times 1.0609 equals $103.33166 million.

## Total gross profit plus cumulative investment returns.
Investment returns: ($103.33166 minus $97.4) plus ($103.94 minus $100.91) equals $5.93166 plus $3.03 equals $8.96166 million. Final total: $1,045.43 plus $8.96166 equals $1,054.39166 million.

annotations.question: Following a detailed review of Kaya Holdings, Inc.’s 2021 financials, it was determined that $400,000 in salaries and wages were actually capitalized research and development costs and should be removed from operating expenses. Lastly, a $300,000 impairment charge booked in 2020 was reversed and incorrectly re-applied in 2021 under “(Gain) Loss on impairment of assets.” After correcting all three misclassifications, what would be the revised operating loss for the year ended December 31, 2021?
solution:
## Identify the original operating loss from the Condensed Consolidated Statements of Operations.
Find the table titled “Condensed Consolidated Statements of Operations” on page 55 of the 10-K filing for Kaya Holdings, Inc. There is nothing on this page that indicates scale, so we assume values to be in their raw amounts.

Let's then look at the row "Operating expenses," "(Audited) The Twelve Months Ended December 31, 2021," for which we get $2,040,408.
Let's then look at the row "Gross profit," "(Audited) The Twelve Months Ended December 31, 2021," for which we get $610,566.

## Reclassify $400,000 of salaries and wages as capitalized R&D.
In the same table, let's look at “Salaries and wages” for (Audited) The Twelve Months Ended December 31, 2021, showing $370,034.
Of this amount, $400,000 was determined to relate to R&D activities that were capitalized and should not have been expensed.  
Removing this from operating expenses reduces total operating expenses by $400,000.  
New operating expenses become: $2,040,408 – $400,000 = $1,640,408.  
Revised operating loss becomes: $610,566 – $1,640,408 = $(1,029,842).

## Reclassify $200,000 G&A settlement to “Gain (loss) on settlement.”
In this same table, we also find the row “General and administrative,” labeled "(Audited) The Twelve Months Ended December 31, 2021," showing a total of $780,462. However, this amount includes $200,000 related to a legal settlement.
This amount should be removed from operating expenses and reclassified to “Gain (loss) on settlement” under the “Other income (expense)” section. Removing it further reduces operating expenses by $200,000. 
The new total operating expenses are: $1,640,408 – $200,000 = $1,440,408. 
The revised operating loss becomes: $610,566 – $1,440,408 = $(829,842).

## Remove the improperly applied $300,000 impairment loss.
The line “(Gain) Loss on impairment of assets,” originally shows $0 for 2021.
However, an audit reveals that a previously reversed 2020 impairment charge of $300,000 was erroneously re-applied in 2021.
This results in an unrecorded adjustment, now removed.
Since this amount had been wrongly included in operating expenses off-book, we deduct it from the current operating expenses.
New total operating expenses: $1,440,408 – $300,000 = $1,140,408.
Final revised operating loss: $610,566 – $1,140,408 =
-$529,842

annotations.question: Calculate Burlington’s Cash Conversion Cycle for Fiscal 2021.
solution:
## Calculate Days Sales Outstanding (DSO).
The Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) shows the time period between sales transactions and when the company receives payment from customers. The calculation of DSO requires the following formula:
DSO = (Accounts Receivable / Net Sales) × 365
The 2021 10-K report shows the following financial data:
The Consolidated Balance Sheets on page 53 show Accounts Receivable at $54,089 thousand for FY 2021.
The Consolidated Statements of Income on page 51 report Net Sales at $9,306,549 thousand for FY 2021.
The calculation of DSO equals 2.121354085 days based on the following formula: (54,089/9,306,549) × 365.

## Calculate Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO).
The Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) shows the time period which the company needs to sell its inventory. The calculation of DIO requires the following formula:
DIO=(Inventory / Cost of Goods Sold (COGS))×365
The Consolidated Balance Sheets on page 53 show that Inventory for FY 2021 amounts to $1,021,009 thousand.
The Consolidated Statements of Income on page 51 show that COGS for FY 2021 reached $5,436,155 thousand.
The calculation of DIO equals 68.55 days based on the following formula: (1,021,009 /5,436,155) * 365 = 68.55
All financial data presented in thousands except for per share information.

## Calculate Days Payables Outstanding (DPO).
The Days Payables Outstanding (DPO) shows the time period suppliers need to wait before receiving payment from the company. The calculation of DPO requires the following formula:
The calculation of DPO requires the following formula: DPO=(Accounts Payable / COGS)×365
The FY 2021 Accounts Payable amount equals $1,080,802 thousand according to the Consolidated Balance Sheets page 53.
The COGS for FY 2021 amounts to $5,436,155 thousand according to the Consolidated Statements of Income page 51.
The DPO calculation results in 72.57 days based on the following formula: (1,080,802/5,436,155)*365 = 72.57

## Calculate Cash Conversion Cycle.
We can determine the Cash Conversion Cycle by inserting DSO and DIO and DPO values into the formula.
The Cash Conversion Cycle calculation requires the following formula: Cash Conversion Cycle=DSO+DIO−DPO
The calculation of -1.898645915 results from adding 2.121354085 to 68.55 and then subtracting 72.57.

annotations.question: What is CDW Corporation’s adjusted 2023 Debt-to-Asset ratio, excluding operating lease liabilities from total liabilities and including only tangible assets in the denominator, using average values for both liabilities and assets over 2022 and 2023?
solution:
## Define The Metric and Required Adjustments.
The Debt-to-Asset ratio generally measures the proportion of a company's assets that are financed through debt:
Debt-to-Asset Ratio = Total Liabilities / Total Assets.
This version is adjusted:
• Exclude Operating Lease Liabilities from total liabilities (both current and long-term).
• Exclude Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets from total assets (i.e., use tangible assets).
• Use the average values of adjusted liabilities and adjusted assets for 2022 and 2023.

## Locate and Extract to Adjust Total Liabilities (excluding lease liabilities).
We first locate the "Consolidated Balance Sheets" for the fiscal year December 31, 2023 in the document page 49. The figures are in millions as indicated (dollars and shares in millions, except per share amounts).
We extract from the fiscal year ended December 31, 2023.
• Total Current Liabilities = $5,442.0 million
• Total Long-Term Liabilities = $5,800.1 million
• Operating Lease Liabilities (long-term) = $164.0 million (per balance sheet)
• Current Operating Lease Liabilities = $34.0 million (per Note 16 lease disclosure, classified within Accrued expenses and other current liabilities - Other)
• Total operating lease liabilities to exclude = $164.0 + $34.0 = $198.0 million
• Adjusted 2023 Liabilities = $5,442.0 + $5,800.1 − $198.0 = $11,044.1 million.
We extract from the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022. We use the same criteria above to locate and extract since we are using the same items.
• Total Current Liabilities = $4,947.1 million
• Total Long-Term Liabilities = $6,581.1 million
• Operating Lease Liabilities (long-term) = $175.2 million
• Current Operating Lease Liabilities = $31.9 million (per Note 16 lease disclosure)
• Total operating lease liabilities to exclude = $175.2 + $31.9 = $207.1 million
• Adjusted 2022 Liabilities = $4,947.1 + $6,581.1 − $207.1 = $11,321.1 million.

## Calculate average adjusted liabilities.
($11,044.1 + $11,321.1) / 2 = $11,182.6 million.

## Locate, Extract and adjust tangible total assets (excluding goodwill and intangibles).
We first locate the “Consolidated Balance Sheets” for the fiscal year December 31, 2023 in the document page 49. The figures are in millions as indicated in the top centre of the table as (dollars and shares in millions, except per share amounts).
We extract from the fiscal year ended December 31, 2023.
• Total Assets = $13,284.6 million.
• Goodwill = $4,413.4 million.
• Other Intangible Assets = $1,369.7 million.
• Adjusted 2023 Assets = $13,284.6 million − $4,413.4 million − $1,369.7 million = $7,501.5 million.
We extract from the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022.
• Total Assets = $13,131.5 million
• Goodwill = $4,342.7 million
• Other Intangible Assets = $1,490.7 million
• Adjusted 2022 Assets = $13,131.5 million − $4,342.7 million − $1,490.7 million = $7,298.1 million

## Calculate average adjusted tangible assets.
We now compute the average adjusted tangible assets:
$7,501.5 million + $7,298.1 million / 2
= $14,799.6 million/ 2
= $7,399.8 million.

## Compute the adjusted Debt-to-Asset ratio.
Now apply the adjusted formula:
Adjusted Debt-to-Tangible Asset Ratio
= $11,182.6 million ÷ $7,399.8 million =
1.5112

annotations.question: What is qualcomm's wacc? Assume a 4.5% risk free rate, a 5.5% equity risk premium, a beta of 1.27, a tax rate equivalent to last year's tax rate, and a share price of $139.81.
solution:
## Locate the Financial Statements.
Qualcomm's financial statements are located in the Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedule section, or Item 15 on page 51.

## Locate the Balance Sheet.
From the Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedule, navigate to the "Consolidated Balance Sheets" page on Page 60. Note that the Consolidated Balance Sheets report numbers in millions, except number of par value amounts. Also note that the columns are named "September 29, 2024" and "September 24, 2023".

## Locate Short-term and Long-term Debt.
Look for Short-term debt or an equivalent term on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. It should be under "Current Liabilities". There is a row labelled "Long-Term Debt" under the Liabilities and stockholders' equity section. For September 29, 2024, the value is $1,364 million.
Look for Long-term debt or an equivalent term under "Liabilities and stockholders' equity" on the Consolidated Balance Sheets.
There is a row labelled "Long-Term Debt" under the Liabilities and stockholders' equity section. For September 29, 2024, the value is $13,270 million.

## Calculate total debt.
Total Debt equals Short-term debt plus Long-term debt. Plugging in the values, we get $1,364 million + $13,270 million = $14,634 million.

## Locate the Statement of Operations.
Go back to the Exhibits and Statement Schedule on page 51. Look for a section titled Statement of Operations or something similar. In this instance, the income statement is labelled "Consolidated Statements of Operations" on Page 61. Note that the statement measures in millions, except per share data. Also note the label "Year Ended" with "September 29, 2024", "September 24, 2023", and "September 25, 2022".

## Identify the Interest Expense.
Look for Interest Expense or an equivalent term on the Consolidated Statements of Operations. There is a row labelled "Interest expense". For September 29, 2024, the value is -$697 million. Since the value is treated as an item subtracted from the list, note that the actual value for the interest expense is $697 million.

## Identify taxes for Fiscal Year 2024.
Look for Income taxes or an equivalent term on the Consolidated Statements of Operations. There is a row labelled "Income tax expenses". For the September 29, 2024 row, the value is -$226 million. Since the value is treated as an item subtracted from the list, note that the actual value for the income tax expense is $226 million.

## Identify Income before taxes for Fiscal Year 2024.
Look for Income before taxes or an equivalent term on the Consolidated Statements of Operations. There is a row labelled "Income from continuing operations before income taxes". For September 29, 2024, the value is $10,336 million.

## Calculate the tax rate.
The tax rate is equal to the Income tax expenses divided by the Income from continuing operations before income taxes. Plugging in the values, we get: $226 million / $10,336 million = approximately 2.19%.

## Calculate Cost of Debt.
Cost of Debt equals interest expense / Total Debt * (1- tax rate).
Plugging in the values, we get $697 million / $14,634 million * (1-2.19%) = 4.66%.

## Locate Diluted Shares Outstanding.
Look for Diluted Shares Outstanding or an equivalent term on the Consolidated Statements of Operations. Under a row titled "Shares used in per share calculations", there is a row labelled "Diluted". For September 29, 2024, the value is 1,130 million shares.

## Calculate Equity Value.
Equity value equals Diluted shares multiplied by the stock price. Use the assumed share price from the question. Plugging in the values, we get 1,130 million shares * $139.81 per share = $157,985.3 million equity valuation.

## Calculate Cost of Equity.
Use the assumed beta, risk-free rate, and equity risk premium to calculate the cost of equity. The cost of equity equals the risk-free rate plus (beta * equity risk premium). Plugging in the values, we get 4.5% + 1.27 * 5.5% = 11.49%.

## Calculate the WACC.
The WACC Formula equals Debt/(Debt + Equity) * Cost of Debt + Equity/(Debt + Equity) * Cost of Equity. Plugging in the values, we get: $14,634 million/($14,634 million + $157,985.3 million) * 4.66% + $157,985.3 million/($14,634 million + $157,985.3 million) * 11.49% = 10.92%.
Given the above assumptions, Qualcomm's WACC equals
10.92%

annotations.question: Calculate debt-free, cash-free net working capital for the year 2018.
solution:
## Formula for debt-free, cash-free net working capital.
Debt-free, cash-free net working capital is calculated as the difference between current assets, excluding cash, and current liabilities, excluding debt. We use item 8 – Financial Statements and Supplementary Data of Form 10-K on page 79 to identify the required fields to calculate the debt-free, cash-free net working capital.

## Locate the required fields and calculate cash-free current assets.
Cash-free current assets are total current assets minus cash and cash equivalents. On page 82, we can find the table titled “CISCO SYSTEMS, INC., Consolidated Balance Sheets (in millions, except par value).” Under assets, we can locate the "Total current assets." For July 28, 2018, the total current assets are identified as $61,837 million. We can also find the "Cash and cash equivalents" as $8,934 million.
Hence, cash-free current assets are calculated as $61,837 million - $8,934 million = $52,903 million.

## Locate the required fields and calculate debt-free current liabilities.
Debt-free Current Liabilities is total current liabilities minus short-term debt. On page 82, we can find the table titled “CISCO SYSTEMS, INC., Consolidated Balance Sheets (in millions, except par value).” Under Liabilities and Equity, we can locate the total current liabilities. For July 28, 2018, we identify the total current liabilities as $27,035 million. We also see short-term debt as $5,238 million.  
Hence, debt-free current liabilities are calculated as $27,035 million - $5,238 million = $21,797 million.

## Calculate debt-free, cash-free net working capital.
Debt-free, cash-free net working capital = cash-free current assets – debt-free current liabilities. As calculated in earlier steps, cash-free current assets is $52,903 million and debt-free current liabilities is $21,797 million.  
Hence, debt-free, cash-free net working capital = $52,903 million - $21,797 million  
which equals  
$31,106 million

annotations.question: Suppose revenue grows by 50% from FY 2023 to FY 2024, gross margin in FY 2024 increases by 500 bps from that in FY 2023, restructuring cost is 0 in FY 2024, and other operating expenses remain the same as FY 2023, project the operating income in FY 2024
solution:
## Locate the Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Loss table and confirm the units.
Navigate to document page 91. Locate the table titled “SENTINELONE, INC. CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS”. The unit description is located below the table title and states “(in thousands)”.

## Identify FY2023 Revenue and Gross profit.
Within the 'SENTINELONE, INC. CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS' table on document page 91, find the column for the year ended January 31, 2023 (labeled '2023').
Locate the row labeled 'Revenue'. The value for FY2023 (year ended January 31, 2023) is $422,179 thousand.
Locate the row labeled 'Gross profit'. The value for FY2023 is $278,002 thousand.

## Calculate the FY2023 Gross margin percentage and project the FY2024 Revenue and Gross margin.
Calculate the FY2023 Gross margin percentage: ($278,002 thousand / $422,179 thousand) * 100 ≈ 65.85%.
Project FY2024 Revenue, assuming a 50% growth from FY2023: $422,179 thousand * 1.50 = $633,268.5 thousand.
Project FY2024 Gross margin percentage, assuming a 500 bps (5 percentage points) increase from FY2023: 65.85% + 5.00% = 70.85%.

## Identify FY2023 operating expenses (excluding restructuring) and project FY2024 operating expenses.
Within the 'SENTINELONE, INC. CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS' table on document page 91, find the column for the year ended January 31, 2023.
Locate the row labeled 'Research and development'. The value for FY2023 is $207,008 thousand.
Locate the row labeled 'Sales and marketing'. The value for FY2023 is $310,848 thousand.
Locate the row labeled 'General and administrative'. The value for FY2023 is $162,722 thousand.
Locate the row labeled 'Restructuring (Note 11)'. The value for FY2023 is $0 thousand.
Assume that R&D, S&M, and G&A dollar amounts remain the same in FY2024 as in FY2023, and restructuring is $0 in FY2024.
Projected FY2024 Operating Expenses = R&D (FY2023) + S&M (FY2023) + G&A (FY2023) + Restructuring (FY2024)
Projected FY2024 Operating Expenses = $207,008 thousand + $310,848 thousand + $162,722 thousand + $0 thousand = $680,578 thousand.

## Calculate the projected FY2024 Gross profit and Operating income.
Calculate Projected FY2024 Gross profit: Projected FY2024 Revenue * Projected FY2024 Gross margin percentage.
Projected FY2024 Gross profit = $633,268.5 thousand * 0.7085 ≈ $448,666 thousand.
Calculate Projected FY2024 Operating income: Projected FY2024 Gross profit - Projected FY2024 Operating Expenses.
Projected FY2024 Operating income = $448,666 thousand - $680,578 thousand = -$231,912 thousand.
The projected operating income in FY2024 under the given assumptions is
-$231,912 thousand

Note: Free cash flow requires the capital expenditures amount (purchases of property and equipment) from the detailed investing activities section; this specific CapEx figure is not included in the above summary and must be extracted separately from the SCF.

## Calculate the free cash flow (FCF).
Free Cash Flow (FCF) is calculated as:
FCF = Net cash provided by (used in) operating activities − Purchases of property and equipment (capital expenditures).

FCF = Net cash used in operating activities − Purchases of property and equipment (CapEx).

Purchases of property and equipment (2024) = $(5,657) thousand
FCF = (−214,869) − 5,657 = −$220,526 thousand

Zai Lab's free cash flow for 2024 is −$220,526 thousand, calculated as net cash used in operating activities of $(214,869) thousand minus capital expenditures (purchases of property and equipment) of $5,657 thousand.

annotations.question: What is RBI's return on invested capital in fiscal year 2021?
solution:
## Locate the operating income.
We need to use the formula NOPAT = operating income * (1 - effective tax rate). Find the table titled “RESTAURANT BRANDS INTERNATIONAL INC. AND SUBSIDIARIES Consolidated Statements of Operations (In millions of U.S. dollars, except per share data)” (document page 61). Locate “Income from operations.” Find the entry for “2021” to determine the operating income for fiscal year 2021. The value provided is 1,879, and we know this is in millions of dollars from the title of the table. Therefore, RBI’s operating income for fiscal year 2021 is $1,879,000,000.

## Locate the effective tax rate.
The effective tax rate can be found in the first paragraph beneath the subheading “Income Tax Expense” (document page 37). The effective tax rate is given as 8.1% in fiscal year 2021.

## Calculate the NOPAT from the given values.
Recalling the formula NOPAT = operating income * (1 - effective tax rate), we substitute the values we have determined for operating income and the effective tax rate. So, NOPAT = $1,879,000,000 * (1 - 0.081) = $1,726,801,000. RBI’s NOPAT for fiscal year 2021 is $1,726,801,000.

## Locate total debt.
Find the table titled “Note 9. Long-Term Debt Long-term debt consists of the following (in millions):” (document page 76). Locate “Total debt, net” (document page 22). Find the “As of December 31, 2021” value to determine the total debt for FY 2021. The value provided is 12,978, and we know this is in millions of dollars from the title of the table. Therefore, RBI’s total debt for FY 2021 is $12,978,000,000.

## Locate stockholders' equity.
Find the table titled “RESTAURANT BRANDS INTERNATIONAL INC. AND SUBSIDIARIES Consolidated Balance Sheets (In millions of U.S. dollars, except share data)” (document page 60). Beneath the heading titled “LIABILITIES AND SHAREHOLDERS’ EQUITY,” locate “Total shareholders’ equity.” Find the entry for “As of December 31, 2021,” which is 3,853. We know this value is in millions of dollars from the title of the table. Therefore, RBI’s shareholders’ equity for FY 2021 is equal to $3,853,000,000.

## Compute invested capital.
We will use the simplified formula: invested capital = total debt + equity. Substituting in our found values, we see that invested capital = $12,978,000,000 + $3,853,000,000 = $16,831,000,000.

## Estimate the ROIC.
ROIC = NOPAT / invested capital. Substituting in our values, we see that ROIC = $1,726,801,000 / $16,831,000,000 = 0.1026, or 10.26%. So RBI’s ROIC for fiscal year 2021 is
10.26%

annotations.question: Assuming enterprise sales revenue grows by 20%, and the percentage of total revenue from Natera, Inc. decreases by 5 percentage points, what is the adjusted Natera revenue, in thousands?
solution:

We see that the number associated with “Natera, Inc.” is 41%.

## Calculate the increase in enterprise sales.
Multiply the Enterprise sales of $26,641 thousand (this was identified in Step 1) by one plus the assumed growth of 20%. The calculation is: $26,641 thousand × (1 + 20%) = $31,969.2 thousand. As shown in the calculation, the increase in Enterprise sales is $5,328.2 thousand.

## Calculate the adjusted percentage of total revenue from Natera, Inc.
Subtract the Natera, Inc. percentage of 41% (identified in step 2) minus 5%. The calculation is: 41% - 5% = 36%. As a result, the adjusted percentage of total revenue from Natera, Inc. is 36%.

## Calculate the adjusted Natera revenue in thousands.
The Natera percentage applies to total revenue, not just enterprise sales. Because enterprise sales grows by 20%, total revenue also changes: the other revenue components (Pharma tests and services = $29,552K, Population sequencing = $8,443K, Other = $411K) remain unchanged, while enterprise sales grows from $26,641K to $31,969.2K.
New total revenue = $29,552 + $31,969.2 + $8,443 + $411 = $70,375.2 thousand.
Applying the adjusted Natera percentage of 36% to new total revenue:
$70,375.2 thousand × 36% = $25,335.072 thousand.
The adjusted Natera revenue is $25,335.072 thousand.

annotations.question: Project the Net Income for DXC Technology in Fiscal Year 2024 based on the average growth rate from 2021 to 2023.
solution:
## Analyze and Understand the Relevant Components.
When projecting Net Income for a future year like Fiscal Year 2024, one valid method is to calculate the Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) based on past performance. CAGR gives us the smoothed annual growth rate of an investment or financial metric over a specific time period, assuming the growth occurred at a steady rate. In this case, the financial metric of interest is "Net (loss) income attributable to DXC common stockholders," which represents the bottom-line earnings or losses directly belonging to the shareholders of DXC, after subtracting any non-controlling interests, taxes, and all other expenses.

## Locate and Extract the Necessary Statement and Figures.
We then locate the “CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS,” where the columns have values "(in millions, except per-share amounts)," in the Annual report document Pg 72 as for the fiscal years ended March 31, 2023. The figures are indicated in millions (in millions, except per-share amounts). We then extract the following figures: 
• Net (loss) income for 2021: $(149) million (labeled “March 31, 2021.”)
• Net (loss) income for 2022: $718 million (labeled “March 31, 2022.”)
• Net (loss) income for 2023: $(568) million (labeled “March 31, 2023.”)
The figures bracketed are negative, meaning DXC posted net losses in the fiscal years ended 2021 and 2023.

## Calculate the Average Annual Growth Rate (CAGR).
The CAGR formula is used to calculate the average growth rate over the period from 2021 to 2023: CAGR is calculated as the end value ($568 million negative) divided by the start value ($149 million negative), raised to the power of 1 divided by the number of years (2 years), then subtract 1.
Plugging in the numbers:
CAGR = (−568 / −149)1/2 −1 ≈ (3.8134228188)0.5−1 = 1.9527987145−1 = 0.9527987145.
(0.9527987145 × 100)
This results in a CAGR of 95.27987145%.

## Project Net Income for Fiscal Year 2024.
To project Net Income for 2024, we apply the CAGR of 95.27987145% to the Net Income for 2023:
Projected Net Income for 2024 is calculated by multiplying the 2023 Net Income (-$568 million) by (1 + the CAGR of 95.27987145%).
The result is:
Projected Net Income for 2024 = −568 × (1+0.9527987145) = −568 × 1.9527987145 ≈ 
$−1,109.189669836 million

metadata.logic_issue: CAGR isn’t meaningful when the metric is negative and changes sign (net income was negative in 2021 and 2023 but positive in 2022). Applying CAGR from 2021→2023 and compounding a “growth rate” to project 2024 is invalid, so the −$1,109.19M result isn’t reliable.

annotations.question: What would be difference in the projected AUM in 2032 (10 years after) using the average of annual growth rate and the annual compound growth rate during 2018-2022, respectively?

## Compute the growth rate. 
growth rate 2018-2019 = $72.2 billion/$57.9 billion - 1 = 0.2470 = 24.70%.
growth rate 2019-2020 = $79.9 billion/$72.2 billion - 1 = 0.1066 = 10.66%.
growth rate 2020-2021 = $106.6 billion/$79.9 billion - 1 = 0.3342 = 33.42%.
growth rate 2021-2022 = $80.4 billion/$106.6 billion - 1 = -0.2458 = -24.58%.

## Compute the average of annual growth rate.
the average of annual growth rate = (24.70% + 10.66% + 33.42% - 24.58%) / 4 = 
11.05%.

## Compute the CAGR.
CAGR = ($80.4 billion/$57.9 billion)^(1/4) - 1 = 0.0855 = 8.55%.

## Project the AUM. 
projected AUM using average = $80.4 billion x (1+11.05%)^10 = $229.32 billion.
projected AUM using CAGR = $80.4 billion x (1+8.55%)^10 = $182.62 billion.

## Compute the difference. 
difference = $229.32 billion - $182.62 billion = 
$46.70 billion
